title: Voters must not need in-depth technical knowledge of the Sky Protocol to understand an Executive Document
content:
A.1.10.2.4.8.1.4 sets the comprehension floor: "Voters should not require in-depth technical knowledge of the Sky Protocol to understand the Executive Document." Crafters must "avoid including excessive technical details that obscure clarity" and include them "only when they are strictly necessary" — specifically "in emergency or urgent responses when technical details are the primary focus of the proposal," or "for non-urgent technical fixes or housekeeping when technical details are relevant, but should be given lower priority compared to other actions."

The two exceptions are shaped differently, which is the tell. In an emergency, technical content *is* the decision, so it moves to the front. In housekeeping, technical content is real but not what the vote turns on, so it is admitted at reduced prominence. Detail is therefore governed by its decision-relevance, not by its accuracy or completeness.

The reasoning given is that "excessive technical detail can overwhelm voters and obscure the document's primary purpose." That treats technical text as actively costly rather than merely unhelpful — it consumes the attention of the median voter and can bury the action that matters.

There is an unresolved risk in this. Technical detail is also where a misdescribed action would be caught, so filtering it for accessibility narrows what a diligent voter can independently check. The framework's answer is structural rather than editorial: technical verification is delegated to the Spell Reviewers, the Content Liaisons and the Executive Sheet, while the Executive Document optimizes for the voter's decision.
description: A.1.10.2.4.8.1.4 admits technical detail only in narrow cases — urgent responses where it is the primary focus, or housekeeping at explicitly lower priority.
